parsed.explanation: No trans-specific offence: the former impersonation law was removed and presentation is not criminalised. A latent, reportedly unenforced same-sex-conduct statute remains, but under the rubric it is secondary where society is documented as tolerant of trans people, with an embedded third-gender role, chiefly inclusion and a sentencing aggravator for gender-identity-motivated crimes. No documented police targeting, violence pattern, facility ban or border practice. Thin formal visitor recourse and unresolved border/enforcement questions keep it moderately below acceptance-with-working-protections, not in a high-risk tier.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Latent ss.67, 68 and 71 criminalise specified same-sex acts, up to five years headline and seven for keeping a place of resort; overview says not enforced and no prosecution recorded, but use since 2013 is unresolved.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Gender presentation itself is no longer an offence after removal of the former male-impersonating-female provision.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Unenforced statute is tangential for a trans visitor unless used as a police lever; no such use is documented.

care_services.protection: Mental Health Act 2007 prohibits conversion therapy by professionals in relation to sexual orientation; no documented gender-identity equivalent or visitor care protection.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Same-sex conduct remains criminal on the books and government rejected repeal in UPR; this is a secondary sexuality-law factor, not a trans-specific offence.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Sentencing Act 2016 s.7(1)(h) treats gender-identity motivation as sentencing aggravation for a separately charged offence.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Official rejection of decriminalisation coexists with removal of the trans-targeted impersonation offence and official recognition of third-gender people as integral to society.

minors_guardians.interaction: No age-dependent visitor, custody, care or travel rule is documented; minors are not shown to face an additional exposure beyond the latent conduct statute.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No trans-specific violence figure, count or documented targeting by police is in the inventory; none should be inferred from absence.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Overview characterises society as very tolerant of being transgender, supported by long-standing third-gender roles and chiefly inclusion; survey basis and currency are unresolved.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Documented social acceptance lowers escalation risk despite latent law and stated intolerance of homosexuality.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Thin formal recourse is documented: no standalone gender-identity charge in the sentencing provision, no documented visitor-facing anti-discrimination remedy, and border/screening exposure is unsourced.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Sentencing aggravator provides some post-offence recognition; third-gender advocacy and 2026 Pride Week indicate organised community presence, though the latter is single-sourced.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Acceptance and a sentencing aggravator mitigate, but do not substitute for documented operative visitor protections.

anchor_checks.comparison: Similar in having remedies and acceptance but documented clinical refusal, exposure and delay; this dossier has no documented visitor care incident, so it sits above 0.65-B despite thinner formal protection.

Similar in low-to-moderate severity and no credible imprisonment for presentation, but 0.75-C documents trained border practice, counsel and compensation; here border practice is not documented, so it sits below 0.75-C.

Higher because 0.85-A documents explicit equality law, chosen-name documents, independent oversight and disciplinary outcomes; this case has acceptance and a sentencing aggravator but no documented operative visitor protection regime, so it remains moderately below.

parsed.synthesis: Combined regime: one statute book with no subnational variation. The operative trans-specific exposure is low—presentation is legal, the old impersonation offence was repealed, and no targeting or violence pattern is documented. The latent same-sex-conduct statute is the main negative, but it is reportedly unenforced, has no recorded prosecution, and must not out-vote documented tolerance and third-gender integration. Main limits are unknowns: border screening, post-2013 enforcement, facilities and care are not documented, and formal recourse is thin. That makes this moderately below acceptance-with-working-protections, around 0.71, for both solo adults and adults with minors.
